extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and students of literary theory (writers and critics of tragedy and epic)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and judging tragic (and related) poetry: requirements for plot unity, diction, metaphor, thought, chorus, and appropriate word-forms and devices across genres (epic, tragic, iambic, dithyrambic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as an integral actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus too should be regarded as one of the actors; it should be an integral part of the whole, and share in the action, in the manner not of Euripides but of Sophocles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choral songs must pertain to the subject of the piece and share in the action; later poets who make choral songs mere interludes (a practice begun by Agathon) weaken the unity — introducing choral interludes is little different from transferring speeches or whole acts between plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and moral appropriateness of reversals (tragic effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic effect is produced when, for example, the clever rogue is outwitted or the brave villain defeated — events that satisfy the moral sense; such events are probable in Agathon's sense: 'it is probable that many things should happen contrary to probability.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversals and situations should aim to satisfy the audience's moral sense (evoke pity/fear) even when surprising; the poet must manage probability so that surprising events remain convincing and morally satisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Dianoia) — speech must produce effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Thought is included every effect which has to be produced by speech, the subdivisions being — proof and refutation; the excitation of the feelings, such as pity, fear, anger, and the like; the suggestion of importance or its opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought concerns the reasoning and the aims of speeches: constructing proofs and refutations, preparing passions (pity, fear, anger), and indicating importance. These are to be treated as in rhetoric (methodical inquiry) and must be prepared by the poet so that the speech produces the intended effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic incidents should show, not narrate
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic incidents must be treated from the same points of view as the dramatic speeches ... The only difference is, that the incidents should speak for themselves without verbal exposition; while the effects aimed at in speech should be produced by the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dramatization to summary: incidents should make their point through action rather than through external explanation; where effects are to be produced by speech, craft the speech to accomplish them rather than having the Thought revealed apart from the speaker's words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of utterance belong to Delivery (not central to poetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: One branch of the inquiry treats of the Modes of Utterance. But this province of knowledge belongs to the art of Delivery and to the masters of that science. It includes, for instance, what is a command, a prayer, a statement, a threat, a question, an answer, and so forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While poets should understand different speech-modes, mistakes in labeling a speech (e.g. command vs prayer) are matters of delivery rather than of poetic craft; the poet is not to be severely censured for such confusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of style: clear without being mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean. The clearest style is that which uses only current or proper words; at the same time it is mean:—witness the poetry of Cleophon and of Sthenelus. On the other hand, loftier diction uses unusual words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance clarity and elevation: use current/proper terms for perspicuity, and introduce strange/figurative/lengthened forms for distinction. Avoid a style wholly of either extreme: all-meticulous commonness (mean) or all-rare/metaphorical (which becomes a riddle or jargon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate, moderate use of rare words, metaphors, and licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: A style wholly composed of metaphors is a riddle; a diction of strange (or rare) terms is a jargon. A certain infusion of these elements is necessary to raise style above the commonplace, but used without propriety and with the express purpose of being ludicrous they become grotesque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors, rare words, lengthening/contraction, and other licenses sparingly and purposefully. Overuse produces riddles (excessive metaphor) or jargon (excessive strangeness); obtrusive use invites ridicule (examples: comic over-extension or deliberate distortion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Varieties of word-forms and their roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Every word is either current, or strange, or metaphorical, or ornamental, or newly-coined, or lengthened, or contracted, or altered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know and deploy these categories: current/proper (perspicuity), strange (local/foreign usage for effect), metaphorical (transference by genus/species/analogy), ornamental, neologisms, lengthenings, contractions, alterations. Their measured mixture yields distinct but clear diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor — types and principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor is the application of an alien name by transference either from genus to species, or from species to genus, or from species to species, or by analogy; analogy or proportion is when the second term is to the first as the fourth is to the third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the available kinds of metaphor deliberately (genus→species, species→genus, species→species, analogy). Metaphor can supply names where none exist, can deny a property of a term for effect, and is especially powerful when proportionally apt (cup of Dionysus / shield of Ares; evening as the old age of the day). Command of metaphor is a central poetic skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction must suit the genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the various kinds of words, the compound are best adapted to dithyrambs, rare words to heroic poetry, metaphors to iambic. In heroic poetry, indeed, all these varieties are serviceable. But in iambic verse, which reproduces, as far as may be, familiar speech, the most appropriate words are those which are found even in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose word-types to fit the poetic form: dithyrambic = compounds; heroic = rare/lofty diction; iambic = metaphorical but generally prose-like current words. Adjust ornament and strangeness according to meter and genre's relationship to ordinary speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of lengthening, contraction, and alteration to add distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing contributes more to produce a clearness of diction that is remote from commonness than the lengthening, contraction, and alteration of words. By deviating in exceptional cases from the normal idiom, the language will gain distinction; while, at the same time, the partial conformity with usage will give perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply such morphological licenses in measured, exceptional cases to gain distinction without losing clarity. Critics who censure these licenses wholesale are mistaken; obtrusive or indiscriminate use, however, yields grotesque or comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and completeness of plot (one whole action)
rubrics_metrics.description: About narrative in measure and mimesis — myths should be composed as in tragedies: dramatic and concerning one action whole and complete, having a beginning and middle and end ... not compositions of similar histories where no one action is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct plots as a single whole: one action made complete with coherent beginning, middle and end. Avoid sprawling multi-subject narratives or mere sequences of episodes that fail to make a single complete action; episodic inserts (e.g., catalogues, many digressions) can break unity if they do not serve the one action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical knowledge of language-parts relevant to metre and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Language in general includes the following parts: Letter, Syllable, Connecting word, Noun, Verb, Inflexion or Case, Sentence or Phrase. A Letter is an indivisible sound; Syllable is a non-significant sound composed of a mute and a vowel; a Connecting word is a non-significant sound which neither causes nor hinders union of many sounds into one significant sound; and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets must understand these building-blocks because distinctions among vowel/mute/semi-vowel, syllabic composition, connecting words, inflexions, and phrasal unity bear on metre and diction. Detailed metrical and phonetic differences are properly the subject of metrical science, but poets should craft language with these elements in mind.
